text: Head: Idaho Releases Fall Back-to-School Guidelines Subhead: Schools to develop plans with local health districts Writer: Logan Finney Date: 7/12/2020 Words: 798 ----- As schools prepare to welcome students back for the fall semester, the Idaho State Board of Education approved a set of reopening guidelines for the coronavirus pandemic last week. The 34-page “Idaho Back to School Framework” creates a three-level plan based on how severely the virus is spreading with considerations including preventative measures, student instruction, transportation and food service. “Despite the incredible advances in digital learning, you can never replace the value and impact of in-person interaction with a professional, dedicated teacher,” Governor Brad Little said at a Thursday press conference introducing the plan. “The expectation is that schools will not be closed for extended periods of time.” With no community transmission and only isolated cases, the plan recommends that schools remain open with physical distancing and sanitation protocols in place. Facing minimal to moderate transmission, modified or staggered schedules should be put in place to limit the number of students gathered at once. Under substantial community transmission, the framework recommends targeted short-term or extended building closures. It will be up to local officials and health districts to determine which of those criteria their communities meet. “This is a balancing act for schools, meeting the needs of our students while navigating public health challenges,” Little said Thursday. “This framework is an initial step and there is going to be a lot of work, especially at the district and charter level, to reopen schools in the fall for in-person instruction.” Board of Education President Debbie Critchfield said that the framework makes recommendations like encouraging parents to perform temperature checks but leaves policies like mask requirements up to local discretion. For sporting events and practices, the framework defers to guidance from the Idaho High School Activities Association. The document says that any district may need to implement short-term closures if an infected person has been in a school building. It also says that schools should be ready to respond to active COVID-19 cases regardless of the level of community spread. While nothing in the plan is mandatory, the framework is meant to serve as a starting point for school officials as they develop their own plans at the local level. “Already, school districts and charter schools are working with their parents and their patrons and are considering a variety of options for reopening,” said Superintendent of Public Instruction Sherri Ybarra. “The key to success this fall will be that parents and students have choices and options for their learning based on what is best for their situation and in their communities, because every single community in Idaho will look different.” Homedale Superintendent Rob Sauer said that his school district has been working to develop plans in conjunction with Southwest District Health, which covers the counties of Owyhee, Canyon, Payette, Gem, Washington, and Adams. Sauer was a part of the 23-member drafting committee for the framework. “Larger districts have more staff in-house that they can talk to,” Sauer said. “Rural districts like us don’t have as many resources, so the framework helps give a picture of who to talk to in your area and what questions to have.”  He said that Southwest District Health began surveying their school buildings early in the summer. “We’re concerned with our high school and keeping everyone physically distanced,” Sauer said. “We have entry points that are easily congested and have narrow hallways. This becomes a challenge during passing periods.”  Sauer said that right now, he expects 85 percent of Homedale students to return to school in person. However, that could vary as circumstances change in the next month. Before schools closed in the spring, Sauer said, students checked out Chromebooks which they have been able to utilize over the summer. He said that to implement distance learning they may have to check out more computers to families with multiple children, and that he preferred the idea of paper packets for younger students. “If the virus ramps up in our area and SWDH limits what we can do in person in schools, we need to make sure we see our K-6 students in person every school day,” Sauer said. “That may mean we have to get creative with how we use our buildings and facilities.” He said that the school board would begin reviewing the district’s plan this week, which he hopes to have completed by late July or early August. The district also plans to send a survey to families about their educational plans around the same time. “It’s so important for us to do everything we can,” Little stressed at the press conference. “We don’t [want to] have a big asterisk on the years ’20 and ’21 and say these kids were lost in the coronavirus gap. That is not acceptable to me and I don’t think it’s acceptable to the people of Idaho.” ###
